paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from observational data often involves two stages: predicting outcomes and treatment probabilities, then feeding those predictions into a treatment-effect estimator. This paper asks how neural networks in the first stage should be designed so that they improve the final estimate. The downstream statistical task therefore guides the network design and training.

The authors propose two adaptations. Dragonnet is an architecture that uses the statistical sufficiency of the propensity score, the probability of receiving treatment, for estimation adjustment. Targeted regularization changes training to favor models with nonparametrically optimal asymptotic properties. That describes behavior as data grows; the regularizer encourages models with those properties rather than guaranteeing optimal estimates for every dataset.

Studies on causal-inference benchmark datasets report that these adaptations outperform existing methods. The contribution connects neural-network modeling with statistical insights about treatment-effect estimation. It shows how the purpose of the final estimator can inform both the architecture that produces its inputs and the objective used to train that architecture.
neurips-2019-adapting-neural-networks-fo.tldr: Dragonnet and targeted regularization adapt neural networks to improve downstream treatment-effect estimates from observational data.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict a class while assigning probabilities that are too confident. Calibration addresses the reliability of those probabilities. This paper proposes a correction designed directly for multiclass predictions, applicable to classifiers from any model class. It extends beyond temperature scaling, which learns a single corrective factor for the inputs to a neural network's final softmax layer.

The method, Dirichlet calibration, is derived from Dirichlet distributions and generalizes beta calibration from binary classification. Its implementation is straightforward: take logarithms of the predicted probabilities, apply a linear layer, and then apply softmax. This provides a multiclass correction without constructing it from separate pairwise or one-versus-rest binary calibration problems.

Experiments report improved probability predictions across a broad range of datasets and classifiers, measured using confidence-ECE, classwise-ECE, log-loss, and Brier score. The learned calibration parameters also offer information about biases in the original predictions. The method thus provides both a practical probability correction and a way to examine how a classifier's confidence needs adjustment.
neurips-2019-beyond-temperature-scaling-.tldr: Dirichlet calibration provides a directly multiclass probability correction that improves calibration across diverse classifiers and datasets.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction intervals with distribution-free guarantees, traditionally using exchangeable data. This paper extends the methodology to situations where the distribution of input features differs between training and testing. That matters because uncertainty estimates must account for the population on which predictions will actually be used, even when it differs from the training population.

The proposed extension introduces weights into conformal prediction. For the covariate-shift setting studied, it requires the likelihood ratio between the test and training covariate distributions to be known. In practice, the authors also consider accurately estimating this ratio from unlabeled test inputs. The ratio supplies information about how the relative prevalence of inputs changes between the two populations.

The theoretical framework extends more broadly to data satisfying a weighted form of exchangeability. The authors also discuss latent-variable and missing-data problems as potential applications. These are proposed directions, while the central result establishes weighted conformal prediction under the stated distributional structure and likelihood-ratio requirement.
neurips-2019-conformal-prediction-under-.tldr: Weighted conformal prediction extends distribution-free intervals to covariate shift when the relevant likelihood ratio is known.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning seeks a measure of separation that reflects the structure of data. Conventional approaches often project data into a feature space and apply a fixed distance function there. This paper argues that such methods fail to capture the underlying geometry needed to represent intrinsic distances, and proposes learning curved measuring structures instead.

The starting point is a reinterpretation of linear distance metrics. The authors show an equivalence with accumulated arc lengths between the nearest points on learned straight measuring lines. They then extend these lines to curves, creating Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning. The curves allow the learned measure to adapt to nonlinear geometry in the training data.

Using the Weierstrass theorem, the authors express the method through a third-order tensor and develop an algorithm to learn its parameters. They provide theoretical analysis supporting the formulation and report better performance than state-of-the-art metric-learning models on synthetic and real datasets. The contribution makes the geometry of the measuring structure itself part of what is learned.
neurips-2019-curvilinear-distance-metric.tldr: Curvilinear Distance Metric Learning replaces straight measuring structures with learned curves to capture nonlinear data geometry.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of a low-rank matrix when each column has been compressed so severely that it cannot be recovered alone. The useful information lies in the shared structure across columns. The authors develop a method that exploits this joint structure to reconstruct the whole matrix from the compressed observations.

Their recovery guarantee bounds relative error in the Frobenius norm, which measures overall matrix error. For rank r and dimensions d1 and d2, the required observation count is O(r(d1 + d2) log^6(d1 + d2) / epsilon^2). The guarantee applies uniformly to incoherent matrices of rank r, so that stated structural condition is part of the result.

The method combines a new mixed-norm with the maximum column l2 norm in a convex relaxation tailored to the observation model. The authors also connect the mixed-norm, nuclear norm, and max-norm through tensor-norm regularization. A scalable ADMM algorithm and large-scale simulations complement the recovery theory with an implementation and empirical assessment.
neurips-2019-decentralized-sketching-of-.tldr: A mixed-norm convex method recovers incoherent low-rank matrices by combining information across individually overcompressed columns.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across training tasks to help a model adapt quickly to new tasks. This paper focuses on learning a shared prior hypothesis for that purpose. It is motivated by difficulties in implementing and analyzing model-agnostic meta-learning, particularly when first-order approximations avoid Hessian calculations but leave convergence and generalization guarantees unclear.

The proposed method uses minibatch proximal updates. Within each task, learning minimizes minibatch risk while being regularized toward the shared prior. The prior is trained so that these updates can quickly approach the optimal hypothesis for each training task. This makes the shared hypothesis useful through the adaptation process it supports.

The authors show that stochastic gradient descent can optimize the prior-training objective with convergence guarantees for convex and nonconvex problems. They also theoretically justify the prior's benefit for adapting to new few-shot tasks. Experiments on few-shot regression and classification report advantages over state-of-the-art methods, combining practical comparisons with an explicitly analyzed adaptation procedure.
neurips-2019-efficient-meta-learning-via.tldr: Minibatch proximal meta-learning learns a shared prior for fast task adaptation with convergence guarantees and few-shot empirical gains.

paragraphs: Graph applications often require both learning missing information and making an optimized decision. Community detection, facility location, and maxcut can all involve graphs that are only partly observed. A conventional pipeline first predicts missing links or attributes and then solves the optimization problem, treating the two stages as separate tasks.

The paper proposes decision-focused learning that connects them through a differentiable optimization proxy. A learned representation maps the original graph problem into a simpler problem through which training can efficiently differentiate. This proxy becomes a layer within the learned system, allowing the optimization task to influence the representation used to support it.

The resulting system, ClusterNet, outperforms both separate learning-and-optimization pipelines and systems that directly predict an optimal solution in the reported experiments. The findings support using an optimization-aware intermediate representation. Its purpose is to make a difficult graph decision accessible to learning through a tractable proxy, while retaining an explicit connection to the downstream optimization problem.
neurips-2019-end-to-end-learning-and-opt.tldr: ClusterNet trains graph representations through a differentiable optimization proxy, improving decisions in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the entropy of a distribution from a stream of samples when memory is tightly limited. The distribution has k possible outcomes, and the target is an estimate within epsilon of its entropy. The central question is how much sampling is needed when the algorithm cannot keep a large memory state.

The proposed algorithm uses a constant number of memory words and O(k log^2(1/epsilon) / epsilon^3) samples. It divides the probability range from zero to one into intervals and estimates the entropy contribution associated with each interval. The interval design balances bias and variance, organizing the estimation around ranges of probability values.

Without memory limits, the established optimal sample complexity is sublinear in k, but existing algorithms achieving it require nearly linear space in k. The paper therefore establishes a different resource tradeoff: entropy estimation with constant-word memory at the stated sampling cost. It also identifies distribution estimation and testing under memory constraints as an area for further research.
neurips-2019-estimating-entropy-of-distr.tldr: An interval-based streaming algorithm estimates distribution entropy within additive epsilon using only a constant number of memory words.

paragraphs: Point-cloud semantic segmentation assigns a semantic label to each point in a three-dimensional collection. This paper builds point representations that incorporate both nearby structure and information from the wider point cloud. Its central idea is that a point's representation should be enriched by context before the model makes its final labeling decision.

The model first applies gated fusion to combine a point's own information with information from contextual points. A graph PointNet module then uses graph attention to compose and update representations within local structures. Finally, spatial-wise and channel-wise attention incorporate global structure, bringing broader context into the representations used to produce semantic labels.

Experiments on S3DIS and ScanNet report performance above state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the proposed combination of contextual fusion, local graph processing, and global attention. The architecture gives each of these stages a specific role: enriching individual points, modeling local relationships, and using information across the point cloud to support the final segmentation.
neurips-2019-exploiting-local-and-global.tldr: Contextual fusion, local graph attention, and global attention improve point-cloud semantic segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet.

paragraphs: Visual commonsense reasoning requires a system to answer questions about images and provide convincing reasoning. This involves aligning visual concepts with language while also reasoning about their relationships. The paper addresses both needs with heterogeneous graphs, which connect different kinds of information rather than representing only relationships among visual objects.

The Heterogeneous Graph Learning framework combines reasoning within graphs and across graphs. A vision-to-answer module and a question-to-answer module interactively refine reasoning paths so that their meanings agree. A contextual voting module additionally brings in long-range visual context, supporting reasoning that uses information beyond the immediate visual relationships.

On the Visual Commonsense Reasoning benchmark, the authors report accuracy improvements of 5% for question-to-answer, 3.5% for question-and-answer-to-rationale, and 5.8% for the combined task. The reported improvements cover all three tasks. They support the framework's approach of coordinating visual and linguistic relationships while incorporating broader image context into the reasoning process.
neurips-2019-heterogeneous-graph-learnin.tldr: Heterogeneous graph learning connects visual and linguistic reasoning and improves all three Visual Commonsense Reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adagrad and Adam maintain statistics for individual model parameters. These statistics help adapt learning, but they also consume memory alongside the model itself. In large translation and language models, that overhead can restrict both the number of parameters and the number of examples processed in a minibatch.

This paper proposes an adaptive optimization method with substantially reduced memory overhead while retaining the benefits of per-parameter adaptivity. The practical aim is to free capacity for larger models and larger batches. The contribution treats the optimizer's stored information as a resource that directly affects which training configurations are feasible.

The authors provide convergence guarantees and demonstrate the method on very large translation and language models. They report speedups of up to twofold compared with the state of the art. This is an observed upper improvement in their evaluation. Together, the theory and experiments support reducing optimizer memory while preserving useful adaptive behavior and enabling more efficient large-model training.
neurips-2019-memory-efficient-adaptive-o.tldr: A memory-efficient adaptive optimizer supports larger models and batches, with convergence guarantees and reported speedups of up to twofold.

paragraphs: Vanishing-point detection relies on the geometry of lines in images. Conventional convolutional networks aggregate edge features but lack a direct mechanism for exploiting the line relationships that define vanishing points. NeurVPS introduces a geometry-inspired operator into an end-to-end trainable network so that this structure becomes part of feature extraction.

The key construction is a conic space in which global vanishing-point geometry can be processed locally. The proposed conic convolution can be implemented as ordinary convolution within that space. It explicitly organizes feature extraction and aggregation along structural lines, while using the same number of parameters as a regular two-dimensional convolution.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significant improvements in vanishing-point detection over traditional methods. The contribution links a geometric reformulation with a familiar neural-network operation: changing the space in which convolution operates allows local computation to capture the relevant global structure. The parameter-count result also shows that this operator introduces geometric structure without increasing the convolution's number of learned parameters.
neurips-2019-neurvps-neural-vanishing-po.tldr: NeurVPS uses conic convolution to incorporate vanishing-point geometry and improve detection without increasing convolutional parameter counts.

paragraphs: Fairness-aware learning often assumes that the sensitive group information in training data is reliable. That can fail when people conceal or obscure their identities, including out of concern about discrimination. This paper asks whether classifiers can still be learned fairly when the sensitive features themselves are noisy.

The answer is positive under two specific conditions: fairness is measured by the mean-difference score, and noise follows the mutually contaminated learning model. Under that setup, a mathematical identity shows that the required correction is a change to the desired fairness tolerance. The needed tolerance can be estimated using existing noise-rate estimators from research on noisy labels.

The authors evaluate the procedure in two case studies involving censoring of sensitive features and report that it is empirically effective. The result provides a concrete way to adapt a fairness constraint to unreliable group information. Its scope is tied to the stated fairness measure and noise model, which make the tolerance adjustment mathematically justified.
neurips-2019-noise-tolerant-fair-classif.tldr: Under a specified noise model and mean-difference fairness measure, noisy sensitive features can be handled by adjusting fairness tolerance.

paragraphs: Pure exploration means gathering observations sequentially to answer a question about an uncertain environment. The objective is to use few samples while making few mistakes. For multi-armed bandits with exponential-family observations, lower bounds characterize the needed sample count through an optimization problem. Existing asymptotically optimal methods repeatedly solve an estimated version of that problem.

This paper interprets the optimization problem as an unknown game. Its sampling rules use iterative strategies to estimate the game and approach a saddle point. No-regret learners drive this process, allowing the algorithm to progressively refine its sampling decisions as information arrives rather than fully solving the estimated optimization problem at each step.

The authors obtain finite-confidence guarantees adapted to the exponential family, covering any pure-exploration query and bandit structure within their setting. Their algorithms require only a best-response oracle. The contribution therefore combines guarantees beyond the asymptotic regime with a different computational approach to choosing samples, using repeated game updates to pursue the information allocation identified by the theory.
neurips-2019-non-asymptotic-pure-explora.tldr: Game-based sampling rules provide finite-confidence pure-exploration guarantees using best-response oracles instead of repeatedly solving full optimization problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover hidden clusters in networks governed by the Stochastic Block Model when node-pair interactions can be sampled sequentially. The learner chooses what to observe and then estimates the clusters. Sampling and clustering are treated jointly because the observations selected determine how much useful information is available for recovery.

The authors derive information-theoretic upper bounds on cluster recovery rates. These bounds identify an optimal sequential sampling strategy that depends on the model parameters, but not on the sampling budget. Their algorithm spends an initial fraction of its budget estimating those parameters and learning the strategy, then uses that strategy to direct the remaining observations.

The resulting algorithm matches the recovery-rate upper bounds. Analytical and numerical results show substantial benefits over random sampling. In particular, the authors prove that adaptive sampling expands the region of model parameters where asymptotically exact recovery is possible. The result demonstrates that choosing observations adaptively can change which clustering problems are recoverable within this model.
neurips-2019-optimal-sampling-and-cluste.tldr: Joint adaptive sampling and clustering achieves optimal recovery rates and expands asymptotically recoverable regimes in the Stochastic Block Model.

paragraphs: Some time series contain statistical asymmetries that make their forward and backward directions distinguishable. Machine-learning methods can exploit such patterns to infer temporal direction. This paper asks whether people can also perceive these subtle differences in motion, connecting a statistical causal-inference question with the study of human visual judgment.

The experiments use autoregressive motion with independent, non-Gaussian additive noise. Human observers can discriminate its forward and backward versions. A frozen-noise paradigm allows trial-by-trial comparisons with four computational approaches: a causal-inference algorithm using noise dependence, a neurally inspired network, a Bayesian ideal observer, and a simple heuristic.

The results suggest that the human observers use similar cues or strategies to one another. However, their behavior differs significantly from the three machine models, with the simple heuristic appearing most similar to human performance. The finding supports human sensitivity to temporal asymmetry in this setting, while the comparative results point toward a heuristic account of the observed judgments.
neurips-2019-perceiving-the-arrow-of-tim.tldr: Humans distinguish forward from backward non-Gaussian autoregressive motion, with judgments most closely resembling a simple heuristic.

paragraphs: Statistical testing often uses sensitive information about individuals, making privacy part of the algorithm-design problem. This paper studies distribution property testing under differential privacy. The goal is to decide whether a distribution has a specified property while using samples efficiently and providing the required protection for individual data.

The authors address two tasks. One tests whether two distributions are equivalent when the available sample counts differ between them. The other tests whether two random variables are independent. For both problems, they construct private testers with sample complexity that is near optimal up to logarithmic factors.

A central result is that dependence on the privacy parameter appears as an additive term in the sample requirement. The authors interpret this as allowing privacy essentially for free in most parameter regimes: the privacy-related term need not dominate the overall sample cost. This is a statement about the sample-complexity tradeoff, with the benefit depending on the regime in which the test operates.
neurips-2019-private-testing-of-distribu.tldr: Private equivalence and independence testers achieve near-optimal sample complexity with an additive privacy-related cost.

paragraphs: This paper changes the output transformation and training loss of a neural network to improve robustness to noise. The method introduces two temperature parameters into the mathematical functions used by logistic loss. One modifies the exponential function underlying the output layer, while the other modifies the logarithm used to evaluate the training loss.

The output layer uses a high-temperature generalization of softmax, and the loss uses a low-temperature logarithm. Tuning both parameters produces a family of losses that can be nonconvex even for a single-layer model. The construction is based on Bregman divergences, giving the two modifications a shared mathematical foundation.

The authors visualize how the temperatures affect behavior in a simple setting and demonstrate efficacy on large datasets. They report more noise-robust training when using the proposed final-layer and loss formulation, as well as superiority to a related two-temperature approach based on Tsallis divergence. The contribution provides two adjustable components for shaping the training objective and improving its empirical response to noise.
neurips-2019-robust-bi-tempered-logistic.tldr: A Bregman-based loss with separate output and loss temperatures makes neural-network training more robust to noise.

paragraphs: Hard-attention image classifiers make decisions using selected portions of an image. Those selections offer some interpretability because they expose the regions used by the model. However, learning where to look from class labels alone is challenging, and such models have been difficult to scale to complex image-classification datasets.

The paper introduces Saccader, a hard-attention model whose central ingredient is a pretraining stage requiring only class labels. This stage supplies initial attention locations for subsequent policy-gradient optimization. It gives the attention-learning process a starting point obtained from the same type of supervision used for classification.

The best reported models achieve 75% top-1 and 91% top-5 accuracy on ImageNet while attending to less than one-third of the image. These results narrow the gap to common ImageNet baselines. The contribution shows that class-label-based pretraining can support effective hard attention at this scale, while preserving the model's use of selected image regions as part of its decision process.
neurips-2019-saccader-improving-accuracy.tldr: Saccader uses class-label-only pretraining to improve hard attention, reaching 75% ImageNet top-1 accuracy while attending to under one-third of each image.

paragraphs: Planning in a partially observable Markov decision process requires decisions based on uncertainty about the current state. This paper proposes an online planning algorithm built around aggregate simulation. It approximates the belief state with product distributions and represents an approximate action-value function as a graph over the space of beliefs.

The graph symbolically captures simulations of the model under independence assumptions. Sampling networks, which represent the process of sampling observations, are integrated into that graph to handle large observation spaces. The resulting representation supports action selection through gradient optimization, connecting the simulation structure directly to the search for a useful action.

The approach complements methods that represent beliefs with particles and select actions through explicit search. It is designed to scale across large state and observation spaces as well as large factored action spaces. Experiments report strong performance relative to state-of-the-art algorithms on large POMDP problems. The product-distribution approximation and independence assumptions are central to how the aggregate representation is constructed.
neurips-2019-sampling-networks-and-aggre.tldr: Aggregate simulation and sampling networks enable gradient-based POMDP planning with large state, observation, and factored action spaces.

paragraphs: This paper develops a decision-making model that first predicts outcomes under each possible action and then uses those predictions to select a randomized policy. The predictive component is intended to combine robustness with the ability to capture nonlinear patterns. The final objective concerns the future outcome of the chosen decision.

The method combines K-nearest-neighbor regression with a new regularized regression technique derived from distributionally robust optimization. The latter uses a Wasserstein-based ambiguity set to represent distributional uncertainty. The authors establish out-of-sample performance guarantees for the predictive model and prove optimality of the randomized policy in terms of the expected true future outcome within their formulation.

On a hypertension dataset, the method's prescribed treatment produces a larger reported reduction in systolic blood pressure than the alternatives considered. The authors also derive a clinically meaningful threshold for activating the randomized policy under a sub-Gaussian assumption on predicted outcomes. The paper thus connects robust prediction, a theoretically analyzed decision rule, and a specific empirical application.
neurips-2019-selecting-optimal-decisions.tldr: Robust nearest-neighbor prediction guides a randomized decision policy with theoretical guarantees and a hypertension-dataset demonstration.

paragraphs: This paper formulates graph compression using optimal transport, incorporating prior information about node importance, node attributes, and edges. The formulation supports both directed and undirected graphs. Its dual description uses distributions over nodes, making the support of those distributions—the nodes receiving nonzero mass—the central object of compression.

Choosing that support makes the optimization difficult to solve directly. The authors introduce Boolean relaxations and give conditions under which the relaxed formulations are exact. This conditional exactness matters because it identifies when the more tractable formulation retains the solution of the original problem. The resulting relaxations support algorithms with provably fast convergence.

The paper also supplies an exact O(d log d) algorithm for projecting a d-dimensional vector onto transformed simplex constraints, addressing a specific computational subproblem. In experiments, the compression method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives on graph classification. The work therefore combines a transport-based compression model, theoretical treatment of its relaxations, and evidence of usefulness for a downstream graph task.
neurips-2019-solving-graph-compression-v.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation compresses graphs through tractable relaxations and improves reported graph-classification performance.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic coordinate descent can be limited by the hardware costs of coordinating many threads. This paper begins by examining a state-of-the-art implementation and identifying obstacles to scaling. These include coherence traffic caused by sharing model information across threads and inefficient access to CPU caches, both of which affect actual training time.

The proposed algorithm, SySCD, redesigns stochastic coordinate descent around those system constraints. It has convergence guarantees and scales across many processor cores and NUMA nodes. The approach makes the organization of computation and memory access part of the algorithm's design, linking optimization progress with the costs of executing updates on multicore hardware.

Across the evaluated datasets and CPU architectures, SySCD reports training-time speedups of up to 12 times over an optimized asynchronous parallel SCD method and up to 42 times over the compared GLM solvers. These are maximum reported gains within the evaluation. The results demonstrate that addressing concrete hardware bottlenecks can substantially improve the practical scalability of coordinate descent.
neurips-2019-syscd-a-system-aware-parall.tldr: SySCD redesigns parallel coordinate descent around CPU memory bottlenecks, achieving convergence guarantees and substantial reported training speedups.

paragraphs: Cascading portfolio scheduling chooses an order for trying a collection of algorithms. The schedule is learned from test instances, then applied to future instances until an algorithm succeeds. Computing an optimal schedule is NP-hard in general, even though the strategy has been useful in applications such as QBF solving and ImageNet model generation.

This paper studies whether structural features of the input make optimal scheduling tractable. Its focus is the success relation: which algorithms succeed on which test instances. Through parameterized complexity analysis, the authors establish fixed-parameter tractability by exploiting properties of this relation.

The findings show that both sparseness and density in the success relation can support nontrivial runtime guarantees for finding an optimal schedule. The general hardness result still applies, but these structural cases provide more informative guidance about computational difficulty. The contribution identifies properties of algorithm-instance performance that can be used to obtain exact scheduling guarantees despite the problem's worst-case intractability.
neurips-2019-the-parameterized-complexit.tldr: Structural sparsity or density in algorithm successes enables fixed-parameter tractable approaches to otherwise NP-hard cascading portfolio scheduling.

paragraphs: Hidden common causes make causal discovery from observational data especially difficult. This paper investigates how to recover relationships among latent variables using information in observed measurements. Its central tool is a family of Triad constraints that exploits non-Gaussian structure in the data to locate hidden confounders and determine causal directions between them.

The authors construct a pseudo-residual from three observed variables and test a particular independence relationship. They show that this can identify the direction between the relevant latent variables when causal relations are linear and noise terms are non-Gaussian. These assumptions are essential to the stated identifiability result and explain where the directional information comes from.

The authors argue that Triad constraints reveal more underlying structure than Tetrad constraints in this setting. They use the new constraints in a two-step algorithm for learning causal structure corresponding to measurement models. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the method's effectiveness and reliability, complementing the theoretical result about what the specified independence checks can identify.
neurips-2019-triad-constraints-for-learn.tldr: Triad constraints identify latent causal directions through independence tests under linear relations and non-Gaussian noise.
